In /opt/nxeon (production tree — READ-ONLY, do not edit; read-only Prisma queries only), diagnose why 5 specific blog posts get real Google impression volume but rank so poorly (position 50-90, page 5-9) that they earn zero clicks. These are a bigger opportunity than the position-25 "striking distance" pages, because they have MORE impression volume yet are buried far deeper — meaning big upside if fixable.

Blog posts are DB-backed `BlogPost` rows (Prisma model ~line 1811 in prisma/schema.prisma), rendered by `app/blog/[slug]/page.tsx`, content stored in the DB (query it directly — read title, body/content, and any SEO meta/excerpt fields). The 5 posts (7-day Google Search Console data):

1. `/blog/best-vps-for-wordpress` — 103 impressions, position ~53
2. `/blog/vps-vs-dedicated-server-which-do-you-need` — 97 impressions, position ~86
3. `/blog/vps-vs-dedicated-game-server-hosting` — 88 impressions, position ~60
4. `/blog/vps-vs-cloud-hosting-whats-the-difference` — 81 impressions, position ~85
5. `/blog/how-to-set-up-a-counter-strike-2-dedicated-server` — 54 impressions, position ~50

For EACH post:
- Read the full post from the DB (find the BlogPost row by slug — write a small `npx tsx` temp script under /opt/nxeon/scripts/tmp-*.ts and DELETE it when done, or use `node -e`). Report its actual word count, title, meta title/description, and whether it has structured content (headings, FAQ, tables).
- Diagnose the likely cause of the deep ranking concretely — the honest candidates for a position-50-to-90 page are usually: (a) the page is genuinely thin/short vs what ranks, (b) it barely uses the target query phrasing, (c) it's an orphan with near-zero internal links (check how many other published posts/pages link to it — grep the DB content and the marketing pages for links to each slug), (d) heavy SERP competition where a young low-authority site simply hasn't earned position yet, (e) possible keyword cannibalization (does Nxeon have MULTIPLE posts targeting the same query, splitting authority? — e.g. there are several "vps vs X" posts; check if they compete with each other). Determine which of these actually applies to each page rather than guessing.
- Give a specific, prioritized fix per post.

Also assess the CLUSTER: posts #2, #3, #4 are all "vps vs [something]" comparisons. Is there cannibalization or a missing pillar page? Would a single strong "VPS vs Dedicated vs Cloud vs Shared — which hosting do you need?" hub page that these link up into (or consolidate into) rank better than 4 separate thin-ish comparison posts each ranking at position 60-86? Investigate the actual content overlap and internal-linking structure among them before recommending consolidate-vs-keep-separate.

Note: another agent already diagnosed 5 DIFFERENT posts (the position-23-30 "striking distance" set: what-is-a-vps, best-vps-specs-for-a-palworld-server, best-vps-for-a-small-business-website, how-much-ram-and-cpu-does-a-game-server-need). Do NOT re-cover those — focus only on the 5 deep-ranking posts above.

Report back: per-post diagnosis + concrete fix (5 posts), plus a clear recommendation on the vps-vs cluster (consolidate into a pillar, or keep separate and fix internal linking — with your reasoning). Keep it concrete and grounded in what you actually read in each post.

4	TITLE: Best VPS for WordPress
5	Once a WordPress site gets real traffic, shared hosting starts to creak — slow admin, timeouts under load, and "resource limit reached" emails. A VPS fixes that by giving you dedicated resources and full control of the stack. Here's how to pick one that keeps WordPress genuinely fast.
6	
7	## What makes WordPress fast on a VPS
8	WordPress performance is a chain: PHP execution, database queries, and caching. A good VPS lets you tune all three, which shared hosting rarely does.
9	
10	- **CPU:** WordPress renders pages in PHP. Modern cores mean faster time-to-first-byte, especially for logged-in and WooCommerce pages that skip the page cache.
11	- **RAM:** 2 GB runs a typical blog or brochure site comfortably; 4 GB gives breathing room for a busier site, PHP-FPM workers and object caching; 8 GB+ suits WooCommerce or high traffic.
12	- **NVMe storage:** the database and media library benefit hugely from fast disk. NVMe cuts query latency and speeds up backups.
13	
14	## Pick the right stack
15	Two common choices:
16	- **LEMP (Nginx + PHP-FPM + MySQL/MariaDB):** lean, fast, the default recommendation for performance.
17	- **LAMP (Apache):** flexible with `.htaccess`, slightly heavier.
18	
19	Nginx with PHP-FPM handles concurrency better under load. Our step-by-step [how to install WordPress on a VPS (LEMP stack)](/blog/how-to-install-wordpress-on-a-vps-lemp-stack) walks the whole build, and [how to host WordPress on a VPS](/blog/how-to-host-wordpress-on-a-vps) covers the fundamentals.
20	
21	## Caching is the biggest win
22	Nothing speeds WordPress up more than caching. Layer it:
23	1. **Page cache** (FastCGI cache or a plugin) serves static HTML to logged-out visitors.
24	2. **Object cache** (Redis) speeds up repeated database queries.
25	3. **OPcache** keeps compiled PHP in memory.
26	
27	A quick Redis install:
28	
29	```bash
30	sudo apt update && sudo apt install -y redis-server php-redis
31	sudo systemctl enable --now redis-server
32	```
33	
34	For the full treatment, see [how to speed up WordPress on a VPS with caching](/blog/how-to-speed-up-wordpress-on-a-vps-with-caching).
35	
36	![Deploying a new server with the Nxeon one-click deploy wizard](/blog/screenshots/deploy-wizard.png)
37	
38	## Don't forget security and backups
39	A VPS means you own the security too — but that's a feature, not a burden. Enable a firewall, keep PHP updated, add HTTPS with Let's Encrypt, and back up regularly. Our guide to [securing a WordPress site on a VPS](/blog/how-to-secure-a-wordpress-site-on-a-vps) has a full checklist.
40	
41	## Tune PHP for real traffic
42	The default PHP settings that ship with a distro are conservative — fine for a demo, limiting for a busy site. On a VPS you can raise them, which shared hosting won't let you do. The settings that matter most for WordPress live in your PHP-FPM pool config and `php.ini`:
43	- **`pm.max_children`** controls how many PHP worker processes can run at once. Too few and requests queue under load; too many and you exhaust RAM. Size it to your available memory divided by the average worker size.
44	- **`memory_limit`** — 256M is a sensible WordPress default; heavy plugins or WooCommerce may want more.
45	- **`upload_max_filesize`** and **`post_max_size`** — raise these if you upload large media or import content.
46	- **`max_execution_time`** — bump it for long imports and backups.
47	
48	After editing, reload PHP-FPM with `sudo systemctl reload php*-fpm`. Getting these right is often the difference between a site that handles a traffic spike and one that throws 502 errors.
49	
50	## Managed or self-managed?
51	Running WordPress on a VPS means you own updates, security and backups. That's more control but also more responsibility. You have three broad options:
52	- **Fully self-manage** on an unmanaged VPS — cheapest, most control, most hands-on. One-click images and [automatic security updates](/blog/enable-automatic-security-updates-linux) make it far less work than it sounds.
53	- **Managed VPS** — the provider handles server maintenance so you focus on the site. See [managed vs unmanaged VPS](/blog/managed-vs-unmanaged-vps-which-should-you-choose) to weigh it up.
54	- **Start managed, learn, then switch** as your confidence grows.
55	
56	Whichever you choose, the performance and control advantages over shared hosting remain — you're just deciding who does the maintenance. For the broader case, read [why a VPS beats shared hosting for a growing site](/blog/why-a-vps-beats-shared-hosting-for-a-growing-site).

63	- Insist on **NVMe** and modern CPU.

89	## The core difference

284	=================== how-to-set-up-a-counter-strike-2-dedicated-server ===================
285	TITLE: How to Set Up a Counter-Strike 2 Dedicated Server
286	Running your own Counter-Strike 2 dedicated server means practice servers, private scrims, and community maps that never fill up with strangers. This guide takes you from a fresh Ubuntu VPS to a public CS2 server you control, using SteamCMD and a Game Server Login Token (GSLT).
287	
288	## What you need first
289	
290	- **A Linux VPS:** Ubuntu 22.04 or Debian 12, at least 2 vCPU and 4 GB RAM for a comfortable competitive server. CS2 is CPU-sensitive, so single-thread performance matters more than core count.
291	- **A Steam GSLT:** create one for App ID 730 at [steamcommunity.com/dev/managegameservers](https://steamcommunity.com/dev/managegameservers). Without it your server can run on a LAN but will not appear publicly.
292	- **Open ports:** CS2 uses UDP/TCP 27015 for game traffic and UDP 27005 for clients. You will open these on the firewall below.
293	
294	## Step 1: Create a non-root user and install dependencies
295	
296	Never run a game server as root. Create a dedicated account and install the 32-bit libraries SteamCMD needs:
297	
298	```bash
299	sudo adduser --disabled-password --gecos "" cs2
300	sudo dpkg --add-architecture i386
301	sudo apt update
302	sudo apt install -y lib32gcc-s1 lib32stdc++6 steamcmd curl
303	```
304	
305	## Step 2: Install the CS2 server with SteamCMD
306	
307	Switch to the cs2 user and pull the server files. The CS2 dedicated server is App ID 730:
308	
309	```bash
310	sudo su - cs2
311	steamcmd +force_install_dir /home/cs2/server +login anonymous +app_update 730 validate +quit
312	```
313	
314	The first download is several gigabytes, so give it a few minutes. When it finishes you will have the game binaries under `/home/cs2/server/game`.
315	
316	![Deploying a new server with the Nxeon one-click deploy wizard](/blog/screenshots/deploy-wizard.png)
317	
318	## Step 3: Open the firewall
319	
320	If you use UFW, allow the CS2 ports:
321	
322	```bash
323	sudo ufw allow 27015/udp
324	sudo ufw allow 27015/tcp
325	sudo ufw allow 27005/udp
326	sudo ufw reload
327	```
328	
329	If your VPS provider has a separate network firewall (many do), open the same ports there too, or clients will time out even though the server is running.
330	
331	## Step 4: Start the server
332	
333	CS2 launches through a shell script in the game directory. Paste your GSLT after `+sv_setsteamaccount`:
334	
335	```bash
336	cd /home/cs2/server/game/bin/linuxsteamrt64
337	./cs2 -dedicated -console \
338	  +ip 0.0.0.0 -port 27015 \
339	  +map de_dust2 \
340	  +sv_setsteamaccount YOUR_GSLT_TOKEN \
341	  +game_type 0 +game_mode 1
342	```
343	
344	Game type/mode 0/1 is competitive. Use 0/0 for casual. Once you see the map load, connect from the CS2 console with `connect YOUR_SERVER_IP:27015`.
345	
346	## Step 5: Run it as a systemd service
347	
348	So the server survives reboots and restarts on crash, create `/etc/systemd/system/cs2.service`:
349	
350	```ini
351	[Unit]
352	Description=CS2 Dedicated Server
353	After=network.target
354	
355	[Service]
356	Type=simple
357	User=cs2
358	WorkingDirectory=/home/cs2/server/game/bin/linuxsteamrt64
359	ExecStart=/home/cs2/server/game/bin/linuxsteamrt64/cs2 -dedicated -console +ip 0.0.0.0 -port 27015 +map de_dust2 +sv_setsteamaccount YOUR_GSLT_TOKEN +game_type 0 +game_mode 1
360	Restart=on-failure
361	RestartSec=10
362	
363	[Install]
364	WantedBy=multi-user.target
365	```
366	
367	Enable and start it:
368	
369	```bash
370	sudo systemctl daemon-reload
371	sudo systemctl enable --now cs2
372	sudo journalctl -u cs2 -f
373	```
374	
375	For a deeper pattern that also handles scheduled restarts, see our guide on how to [automate game server restarts with systemd and cron](/blog/automate-game-server-restarts-with-systemd).
376	
377	## Configuring the server
378	
379	Drop a `server.cfg` into `/home/cs2/server/game/csgo/cfg/` with your basics:
380	
381	```
382	hostname "My Nxeon CS2 Server"
383	sv_password ""
384	rcon_password "change-this-strong-password"

392	## Picking the right hardware
393	
394	CS2's 64-tick (or higher, with community configs) simulation rewards fast cores. A 4 GB / 2–4 vCPU plan handles a full 10-player match well; move up if you run 128-tick or multiple servers. 400	- **+tv_enable 1** turns on GOTV so matches can be spectated or recorded as demos.
401	- **-maxplayers_override 12** hard-caps the slot count regardless of the game mode's default.
402	- **+exec gamemode_competitive_server.cfg** loads a competitive ruleset at boot.

405	For scrims, keep match configs in `csgo/cfg` and load them from RCON mid-session — a knife/warmup config, then a `live` config that runs `mp_restartgame 1` and enables overtime. That's how most pug and practice servers switch phases without a full restart.

407	## Troubleshooting a CS2 server
408	
409	- **Starts then quits instantly:** almost always an invalid or missing GSLT. Regenerate the token for App ID 730.
410	- **"Unable to verify" or VAC errors:** re-run `+app_update 730 validate` to repair corrupted files.
411	- **Tick drops under load:** CS2's simulation is single-thread heavy — move to a faster core or lower the tickrate, and watch load with `top`.
412	- **Visible in the browser but times out on join:** the client port (UDP 27005) or a second firewall is blocking traffic.

421	### Why can players not connect even though the server is running?

433	=================== vps-vs-shared-vs-dedicated-vs-cloud-hosting ===================
434	TITLE: VPS vs shared vs dedicated vs cloud hosting
435	Every hosting company sells the same four broad tiers under a hundred marketing names. Once you understand what actually separates them, choosing is easy.
436	
437	## Shared hosting
438	
439	Hundreds of websites live on one server and share its CPU, memory and disk. A control panel manages everything for you; you never see a command line.
440	
441	- **Pros:** cheapest option, zero server management.
442	- **Cons:** no root access, no guaranteed resources, and a "noisy neighbor" spike can slow your site. You can only run what the host allows.
443	- **Best for:** a small blog or brochure site with modest traffic.
444	
445	## VPS hosting
446	
447	A physical server is split by a hypervisor into isolated virtual servers. Each gets **guaranteed** CPU, RAM and NVMe storage plus **full root access**.
448	
449	- **Pros:** private and predictable performance, install anything, your own firewall and OS, excellent price-to-power ratio.
450	- **Cons:** you're responsible for administering it (though one-click panels remove most of that).
451	- **Best for:** growing sites, web apps, developers, self-hosters — the majority of projects.
452	
453	## Dedicated server
454	
455	You rent an entire physical machine. Nothing is shared.
456	
457	- **Pros:** maximum raw performance and total control of the hardware.
458	- **Cons:** most expensive, often overkill, and you wait for physical provisioning.
459	- **Best for:** very high traffic, heavy databases, or strict compliance needs.
460	
461	## Cloud hosting
462	
463	Cloud is really a *delivery model* for VPS-style instances: you spin them up in seconds, resize on the fly, and often pay by the hour. Underneath, each instance is a virtual server much like a VPS.
464	
465	- **Pros:** elastic — scale up for a launch, scale down after; pay for what you use.
466	- **Cons:** costs can creep if you don't watch usage; more moving parts.
467	- **Best for:** variable or spiky workloads, teams that want to scale on demand.
468	
469	## Side-by-side
470	
471	| Feature | Shared | VPS | Dedicated | Cloud |
472	|---|---|---|---|---|
473	| Root access | No | Yes | Yes | Yes |
474	| Guaranteed resources | No | Yes | Yes | Yes |
475	| Isolation | Low | High | Full | High |
476	| Scalability | Low | Medium | Low | High |
477	| Price | $ | $$ | $$$$ | $$–$$$ |
478	| Management | Host | You | You | You |
479	
480	## How to decide
481	
482	Ask three questions:
483	
484	1. **Do I need root access or custom software?** If yes, shared is out.
485	2. **Are my resource needs steady or spiky?** Steady points to a VPS or dedicated box; spiky favors cloud elasticity.
486	3. **How big is the workload?** Small to large fits a VPS. Only very heavy, sustained loads justify a dedicated machine.
487	
488	For most people the honest answer is a VPS. It's the tier that gives you real control and guaranteed performance without dedicated-server pricing.

503	=================== how-to-set-up-a-cs2-server ===================
504	TITLE: How to Set Up a Counter-Strike 2 (CS2) Server
505	Running your own Counter-Strike 2 server gives you a private space for scrims, practice and community matches with the tickrate, maps and plugins you want. Here's how to stand one up on a Linux VPS.
506	
507	## What you'll need
508	
509	- A VPS with **2 GB RAM** for a 10-player match; **4 GB** with plugins and demos.
510	- Low latency to your players — for competitive play, **ping is everything**, so pick a location close to them.
511	- A free **Game Server Login Token (GSLT)** from Steam.
512	
513	## Step 1: Get a GSLT
514	
515	CS2 public servers require a token. Visit steamgameserveraccount.com while logged in, create a token for App ID **730**, and save the string — you'll need it at launch.
516	
517	## Step 2: Install SteamCMD
518	
519	```
520	sudo add-apt-repository multiverse -y
521	sudo dpkg --add-architecture i386
522	sudo apt update
523	sudo apt install steamcmd screen -y
524	```
525	
526	## Step 3: Download CS2
527	
528	```
529	sudo adduser --disabled-password cs2
530	sudo su - cs2
531	steamcmd +force_install_dir ./cs2-server +login anonymous +app_update 730 validate +quit
532	```
533	
534	App ID **730** now serves the CS2 dedicated server. It's a large download.
535	
536	## Step 4: Launch the server
537	
538	CS2's launcher lives a few folders deep. Start a competitive match on Dust II like this:
539	
540	```
541	screen -S cs2
542	cd cs2-server/game/bin/linuxsteamrt64
543	./cs2 -dedicated -console -usercon \
544	  +game_type 0 +game_mode 1 \
545	  +mapgroup mg_active +map de_dust2 \
546	  +sv_setsteamaccount YOUR_GSLT_TOKEN \
547	  +sv_password "" +hostname "My CS2 Server"
548	```
549	
550	The `game_type` and `game_mode` pair sets the format — `0 1` is competitive, `0 0` is casual, `1 2` is Deathmatch, and `0 2` is Wingman. Get this pair wrong and the server loads the wrong ruleset, so double-check it against the mode you want before players connect.
551	
552	## Step 5: Open the ports
553	
554	CS2 uses **UDP 27015** for the game and **TCP 27015** for RCON:
555	
556	```
557	sudo ufw allow 27015/udp
558	sudo ufw allow 27015/tcp
559	```
560	
561	## Step 6: Connect
562	
563	In CS2, open the console (enable it in settings) and type:
564	
565	```
566	connect your-ip:27015
567	```
568	
569	If you set an RCON password with `+rcon_password`, you can administer live with `rcon` commands.
570	
571	## Adding plugins with Metamod and CounterStrikeSharp
572	
573	For custom game modes, retakes, surf or admin tools, install **Metamod:Source** and **CounterStrikeSharp**. These load into the server and open up a huge library of community plugins. Reinstall or update them after each CS2 patch, since Valve updates can temporarily break them.
574	
575	## Useful launch and server settings
576	
577	A few convars make a practice or scrim server much nicer. Set them at launch or in a config file:
578	
579	```
580	+sv_cheats 0
581	+mp_autoteambalance 1
582	+mp_maxrounds 24
583	+sv_hibernate_when_empty 0
584	```

586	Setting `sv_hibernate_when_empty 0` keeps the server warm so players don't hit a stutter when the first person joins. For a dedicated practice server, a separate config with `sv_cheats 1`, `sv_infinite_ammo` and `mp_warmup_end` lets you throw grenades and rehearse executes.
587	
588	## Recording demos
589	
590	CS2 servers can record match demos for review. Use `tv_enable 1` to run GOTV, or trigger a demo with the `record` and `stop` console commands. Demos are invaluable for teams reviewing scrims — store them off-server as part of your backups.
591	
592	## Why location beats everything
593	
594	Counter-Strike is unforgiving about latency — a 20 ms difference is felt in every peek and trade. Host the server as physically close to your players as you can. If your group is spread across Asia-Pacific, a Singapore location is often the best single compromise.
